Introduction & Executive Summary** ##### **1.1 Introduction** Since the release of our previous 3-Year Gold Forecast (27th October 2010), gold has experienced a powerful rally, with the price reaching a new peak of $1,426 in early December. A modest correction followed but the price remained elevated through to the year end. With a 26% year-on-year increase in the average annual price, gold has now registered nine consecutive years of annual gains, an unprecedented record post-1968. Looking at 2010 as a whole, gold’s impressive performance was primarily driven by two waves of investment inflows. Firstly, in response to a worsening of the European sovereign debt crisis during the second quarter, it was not surprising that demand for gold as safe assets surged in May and June in particular. Indeed, fears regarding the potential collapse of the euro saw the bulk of purchases concentrated in physical bullion products and gold ETFs. In contrast, the strong rally in the latter part of 2010 was primarily driven by speculative interests, as evidenced by a substantial increase in long positions in both OTC and futures markets, principally from late August through to October. The main reason behind this change was renewed dollar weakness, itself the result of growing fears over the outlook for long-term inflation, particularly after the US Federal Reserve revealed its QE2 package on 3rd November. Moreover, the United States is not the only country that will maintain a loose monetary policy; Japan announced a cut in interest rates and further quantitative easing in October, while the European Central Bank also stated that it will continue to offer unlimited liquidity to banks. Despite some profit taking towards the year-end, gold remained resilient at this time, helped by growing fears concerning Ireland’s debt, along with increasing tensions in the Korean Peninsula. Furthermore, the extension in mid-December of (then) President Bush’s tax cuts led to renewed concerns over the unsustainability of government debt in the United States, which also helped to limit the scale of long liquidations at end-2010. ###### **~~Price Forecast Comparison~~** |© Copyright GFMS Limited

Several factors will drive this wave of investment. As a result, real short-term interest rates will remain negative, or at close to zero, for an extended period. 

Moreover, we would expect the ultra-loose monetary policy to be accompanied by less enthusiastic efforts from governments to cut their fiscal deficits, particularly in the United States where the country prefers to monetise its soaring budget shortfalls and will therefore be prepared to accept a higher rate of inflation to reduce the real value of government debt. Specifically, there is still a risk that the crisis will spread in 2011 and eventually move to the United States. Finally, despite a widening investor base for gold over the past few years, we would argue that the exposure to gold of so-called “real money” managers is still tiny compared to mainstream asset classes. Last year, net investment inflows into gold were estimated to have totalled $65 billion, representing a lift of just 9% yearon-year. Moving forward, there is therefore tremendous scope for pension funds, insurance companies, sovereign wealth funds and other institutional investors to invest in bullion, particularly given concerns over all major currencies. Nevertheless, the emergence of higher inflation, particularly in the United States (where the CPI is forecast to rise to an average of 3.9% in 2013), will help limit the fall in gold prices that year. We can also project two potential scenarios for the global economy that are very different to our Base Case. In each instance, these would have distinct implications for the level and trajectory of gold prices over the next three years. **Scenario B** (with a 30% probability) presents the most positive outlook for gold prices, with an investor-led bull market continuing throughout the forecast period. Over this ti

The main cause of this is the substantial level of liquidity that has been pumped into the market by the US Federal Reserve from 2008 to 2010.  Furthermore, it is very likely that the authorities will be tempted to tolerate a rise in inflation if this boosts GDP growth and reduces the real level of public debt. These factors should prompt a far broader move into gold among institutional investors, which will result in gold prices advancing in each year of the forecast period to an average of $1,920 in 2013. 

A complete contrast is **Scenario C** (with a 20% probability), where investment in gold will start to decline this year.  Under this variant, after reaching a peak of $1,260 in 2011, the average price then declines, dropping to $1,090 and $960 in 2012 and 2013 respectively.  This is basis a secular recovery in the dollar and a low level of inflation, reflecting governments’ failure to boost private demand and consumer spending in advanced economies. 

The negative impact on gold investment of a prolonged period of low inflation in western countries will be compounded by tighter monetary policy and other administrative measures that will be undertaken in key emerging economies (such as China and India) to combat rising local inflation, which will also drag down the rate of world GDP growth.  These factors should also reduce gold’s appeal to investors, most notably in the final two years of the forecast, when a marked reduction in investment results in prices slipping to levels that are more in line with gold’s underlying supply/demand fundamentals. 

Much of the above discussion has focused on the interplay between changes in the principal economic variables and investment demand.  As mentioned previously, however, we do not subscribe to the view that price direction and level are determined by investment alone.  The following analysis of expected trends in the key supply/demand variables shows that these will also play an important, even if subsidiary, role in gold price determination over the next three years. 

###### **1.2 The Base Case Scenario** 

Looking at **mine supply** , compared to our previous report in October, we now prescribe a more positive result; after hitting a new record of 2,652 tonnes in 2010, mine production under the Base Case is expected to rise by 3% and 2% over the next two years, with output by 2012 reaching 2,765 tonnes.  The growth is underpinned by a robust project pipeline, coupled with rising gold prices, which will extend the life of operations that were originally du

e to close during this period. That said, by 2013 the pipeline will have thinned sufficiently such that declines in production at many established operations will offset the contribution from newly commissioned projects. As a result, mine production is expected to start to fall towards the end of the forecast, albeit marginally. **Scrap** volumes have been revised substantially lower compared to the October forecast, due to such factors as near-market supply exhaustion in the Middle East and evidence of a far lower than expected lift in recycling despite a strong price rally in late 2010. Given that gold is likely to rise above $1,600 at some point this year, we expect scrap supply to register a fresh record high. However, we are only expecting a fairly modest increase of 8% (to 1,779 tonnes) as a result of, for example, dollar weakness limiting gains for some local prices and several markets seeing nearmarket supply depletion. Thereafter, the series broadly follows a downward trajectory in line with our forecast for weaker gold prices through to 2013. Moving to the demand side, **jewellery consumption** is currently forecast to see a drop of 3% in 2011, primarily driven by stronger gold prices, although an improvement in world economic growth will limit the loss. China is again expected to remain an exception as it records further gains. Thereafter, offtake in many countries will start to recover, aside from India, where jewellery consumption is forecast to fall sharply in 2012, leaving the global total down marginally that year before a 6% recovery emerges in 2013. The rebound in the final year should come largely from a strong recovery in price sensitive markets, particularly in India and the Middle East. Nonetheless, the level attained in 2013 of 2,068 tonnes is still well below 2008’s still depressed total. After a major recovery in 2010, **other fabrication** demand will continue to rise over the next two years, thanks mainly to growth in the electronic sector and robust demand for official coins. Notable losses in official coins in 2013 mean, however, that non-jewellery fabrication demand is forecast to fall slightly, although volumes will remain at historically high levels. After being a consistent net seller from 1989 to 2009, the **official sector** switched to become a net buyer of (an estimated) 87 tonnes last year. ### **2.  Price Forecast & Economic Assumptions** 

###### **2.1  Introduction** 

GFMS’ views for the forecast period are presented in the form of three probability-weighted scenarios, namely the Base Case Scenario, Scenario B and Scenario C.  Under our Base Case projections we expect a slowdown in global GDP growth this year, partly as the effect of fi scal stimulus plans ebb, before a gradual pick up in growth occurs over the fi nal two years of our forecast due to improvements in the underlying world economy.  We view this as the most likely scenario and since our October forecast the probability of our Base Case Scenario has remained at 50%. 

Our more bullish Scenario B, to which we assign a 30% probability, predicts infl ation rising over the next three years, albeit modestly at fi rst, above all in the United States.  Central to this scenario are the policies being followed by the US government and the Federal Reserve.  These include a continuation of the very loose fi scal and monetary policy including the second round of quantitative easing.  Such policies are forecast to largely avert a renewed economic slowdown in 201113 but at the cost of rising infl ation, with it reaching an annual average of 5.5% in 2013.  Moreover, the US dollar weakens under this scenario. 

Under our bearish Scenario C, to which we assign a 20% probability, we expect the effect of government measures to be negligible on the longer run growth rate as the global economy struggles to escape defl ation. ###### **4.3 Developing World** 

Scrap supply from the developing world was unable to eclipse the record levels witnessed in 2009, slipping more than 10% in 2010.  The decline may appear slightly counter intuitive given that the dollar gold price increased by almost 26% last year.  However, there were a number of factors that brought about this outcome, the principal ones comprising: supplies being withheld in anticipation of further price gains, price acclimatisation and, in some markets, near-market supply depletion.  The price surge in the final quarter of 2010 did nonetheless provide the opportunity for both consumers and the supply chain to liquidate some assets as consecutive record prices (in a number of currencies) were breached.  However, in some regions, scrap flows remained well below that witnessed in previous years during periods of volatile trading. 

A key characteristic of these price sensitive markets is the dominance of low labour cost and high carat jewellery.  This trait provides the opportunity for gold assets to be immediately returned to the market during periods of elevated gold prices.  Moreover, this low margin structure is the major reason why gold jewellery can often be viewed as an investment vehicle (in contrast to the industrialised world), with consumers willing to “invest” in plain jew

ellery with the clear intention of selling the item back should the gold price move in a favourable direction and a profit be obtained. 

In recent years there has been a notable shift away from this plain, high purity jewellery to more western designs that feature more stones, are often lightweight, and have a far higher labour component, with higher gold prices and economic advancement the two main drivers of this change.  As access to financial products in the developing world has improved, the reliance on gold as a savings vehicle is also diminishing. As a result, younger generations in particular are increasingly looking to lower carat, more intricate stone-set designs as a fashion item, rather than simply as an investment, preferring something that can be worn for everyday use.  However, this trend is only slowly gaining momentum from a very low base, so the impact at this point remains insignificant and unlikely to materially influence emerging markets’ scrap supply within this three-year forecast period.
